content:
Hello,
I've been exploring and analyzing how to help people adopt and see the benefits of formal languages and theorem provers for the last little while. Recently I sort of made it a personal mission to create and publicize some content which will hopefully be able to generate some excitement on the topic.
Lean is obviously top of my mind as one of the tools I want to recommend.

The two things I want to communicate are:

  1. Formal verification and formal languages are fun logical puzzles that will outgrow LLMs.
  2. The benefits of understanding these tools and methods are high.

The main problems I seem to run into are:

  1. Formal languages and methods are extremely complicated and hard to understand.
  2. The benefit of understanding them does not seem to rationalize the effort.

I'm not really here to debate these rhetorical points but happy to do that if the discussion takes that route.
I'm really here looking for ideas and feedback on how to Help newcomers learn and get excited about theorem proving.

recently I worked with an LLM to help generate this draft of a learning roadmap.

I wonder if any newcomers could give me their impressions and maybe thoughts on the approachability of this proposed roadmap. Additionally any veterans that might be able to refine the trajectory and direction of this roadmap are also welcome.

Lean 4 Learning Roadmap_ From Scratch to Mathlib and Software Verification.pdf

Regardless of who you are and what you know:

  1. Why did you initially begin pursuing formal proof and verification?
  2. Why did you continue pursuing formal proof and verification?
  3. Does my proposed roadmap seem approachable or aligned with your own experiences?

Heres the markdown version you can give to an LLM if you want.

Lean 4 Learning Roadmap_ From Scratch to Mathlib and Software Verification.md

I will take your assessment of "1. Formal languages and methods are extremely complicated and hard to understand." as a compliment :see_no_evil: (though its a never ending journey of understanding in all math IMO) .

I know you said you'd rather not debate them (and italics newcomers, though I do still consider myself one), but I do think they are more than just rhetorical. So I would recommend trying to quantify/rationalise the
2a. "The benefits of understanding these tools and methods are high." and
2b. "The benefit of understanding them does not seem to rationalize the effort."

The idea of formalising mathematics symbolically using computer language did come about fairly naturally and near the advent of computing, and it did take a huge amount of CS theoretical development (and of course huge leaps in computational hardware and software) to get us the latest bells and whistles of CIC in Lean.

But latest here is actually fairly late, ROCQ has been around sporting pretty much the same foundations, other theorem provers and such exist etc.

I think you are right in 2b. but I think 2a. is actually harder to justify in itself, especially in the LLM age, and pragmatically as a practical benefit for math academics/practitioners.

All that being said, and this is of course biased, I think the best way to learn lean is to avoid LLMs for a while.

To this day AI lean code is really not ideal or very satisfactory, and I am not sure learning using LLMs will gain the requisite insight esp. for a relatively small corpus and evolving language like Lean.

Ty said:

Regardless of who you are and what you know, what are your thoughts?
Does it seem like something worth trying?

As a general matter I think these resources should probably be written by subject matter experts. There are already some very good resources to try and help newcomers wade into the mathlib waters (see for example mathematics in lean).

I would maybe put the markdown version in a gist and link it so people don't have to download and open an untrusted file.

@Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦
Sorry, I realize I didn't make this clear:
When I stated the problems I seem to run into, what I meant was the common rhetorical rebuttals I often get stonewalled by.

I actually believe that most people don't recognize the benefits that can come from formal methods, languages, and verifications beyond just mathematics and computer science.
All quibbles about LLMs aside, understanding how to formalize a concept is very valuable and has significant benefits in helping people understand problems and possible solutions before the task of actually completing a formalization is even done. In my opinion, this is the greatest advantage and benefit of formalization.

One simple application I tend to point to often is that with LLMs, specificity beats implicitness every time.
Formal languages like Lean or ROCQ require a person to become extremely specific about what they're trying to state. giving that kind of a specification to an LLM is invaluable as a roadmap.
And it works for just about anything that you're trying to get an AI to do. I think we often forget that these are language models, and so it doesn't matter if what we write is human-readable as long as a language model has been trained on it.

I can describe myself throwing a ball at the wall or I can write a formal proof for it. If my objective is to create a robot that can throw a ball at the wall, or even a software ball-throwing simulator, which specification do you think will work better for an LLM?

  • A prose monologue of what it's like to throw a ball at a wall
  • A mathematical statement describing the physics of such an event

Although they may suck at writing formal proofs of nearly any kind, LLMs are great at reading them and translating them. This gives those who know how to write them a massive advantage over people who do not, in pretty much any field.
After all, applied mathematics touches nearly everything temporal, and theoretical mathematics can maybe touch even more applied surfaces abstractly.

Trying to explain this benefit to someone who has written formal proofs before works because they understand what's required and what you can end up taking from the experience. Trying to explain the benefit to someone who has not yet done it is surprisingly difficult.

most of the proofs people write in grade school are not that rigorous or specific and honestly don't actually teach that much other than maybe appropriate syntax structures.

So most of these pro-formalization arguments quickly get reduced to "that seems like overkill."
to the person coming out of grade school proofs, the easy ad absurdum seems to be: "Why wouldn't I just tell an LLM to write a program that makes my robot throw the ball at that wall and just iterate on that 110 or 120 times until it gets within the tolerances I want?"

And to the person who's formalization-curious: a common rebuttal is: "why wouldn't I just tell an LLM to write a proof of me throwing a ball at the wall and then use that as a prompt for the next LLM?"
Which, as we know, would very likely actually be worse than the former.

Responding to questions like these is where the conversation often dies.

Once we say something like, "because formal and machine-checked proofs require a certain level of specificity," the quiet undertone often becomes "so I'll just write more specific descriptions in my AI prompts."

My point on the benefits is never really able to land because, in the end, one can only know the color red if they have eyes to see/feel it.
Likewise, one can only see/feel the benefits of writing a formal proof after doing it themselves.

I don't know how to help people get over that hump, even when they're semi-curious.
The barriers to entry seem high, and the payoff minimal when compared to the methods people typically use. (1b, 2b)

Like I said: I don't mind discussing these rhetorical points. I don't mind discussing them further, even. but the point of this thread is to discuss ways to help people overcome that barrier, specifically for people who are curious or already partially engaged.
Which is why I came to the newcomers channel.

@Ty I would say I personally agree with basically all of that , and such “softer” benefits of formalisation. I happen to be a bit of a fan of it myself .

I just wanted to bring it up I guess to distinguish versus expecting any pragmatic / practical benefit .

But I’d say we are on the same page otherwise, though I didn’t mean that LLMs are necessarily too bad at this. It’s more that their error rate can be dramatically unpredictable , esp. for Lean, when explaining concepts .

LLMs do ironically seem to need a certain touch to do teaching well , and are often better as data handlers for experts who can spot its randomly egregious lies ( all of this is just in my experience ofc ).

@Chris Bailey
Thanks for the gist tip. I'll edit that.

I definitely agree that the subject matter experts, like yourself, should be in charge of the learning materials. Most of the things I've cited are written by subject matter experts, I believe.

My point in coming here was to discuss rhetorical angles for making these learning systems approachable and attractive. For example, roadmap.sh is a really common resource and might be a place someone who is looking to simply write "good specs" ends up.

The thing I want to discuss is actually probably more of a marketing or evangelistic type.

My fear is that someone who is curious or interested in formal methods becomes averse to the idea before they've even really understood it.

I want to find/build a learning path that is simultaneously engaging, intriguing, and approachable to newcomers

One challenge is that the learning journey is highly dependent on what you want to use Lean for.

  • Is it classical software engineering, to do things you'd be able to do with Python/Java/Javascript/etc?
  • Is it software engineering with formal verification?
  • Is it formal mathematics?
  • Something else?

The use surface of Lean is very wide and a new learner can easily conflate scopes. You'd have to pick up your target first.

@Arthur Paulino
I'm targeting the group interested in formalization in either mathematics or software engineering.

Formalizing math and software are two very different beasts.

Math builds up from relatively simple and well-known definitions, arriving at surprisingly interesting theorems. Software builds up from new/involved definitions (like a stack of compiler stages or whatever), arriving at somewhat boring theorems (specifications), whose proofs are very often mechanical unfoldings.

So the actual practice of proving the theorems take very different forms, depending on the domain you're targeting. For a total beginner, picking a specific domain is the first step IMO.

Frankly, as far as I can tell (speaking as a newcomer), Lean already has a friendly learning roadmap between the natural numbers game, mathematics in lean, a very active community here on zulip, etc. I'm not sure getting an LLM to spit out a summary of how to get people involved changes anything or helps anything. If people are interested in actually learning, they'll do it, because the benefits of exploring a new way of thinking are obvious. An LLM roadmap is not going to change how people engage. In fact, LLM content for teaching people/giving advice is often quite off putting in my experience.

I think you are making implicit (and in some cases unwarranted) assumptions about the audience. It would be extremely helpful to state for whom this roadmap is intended.

Suppose I am a student with independent resources (I have enough time and money and space to follow most suggested programs). If I decide I want to set up a software environment to learn about Lean and any track involving Lean (including but not limited to mathematical research or software development verification), I may find your roadmap helpful. More likely I might find the TL;DR section most helpful.

Suppose I am a person looking for employment (I have a limited amount of time and resources) and I think I might be able to get a job doing verification of systems, and that I seek employers who are looking for Lean expertise. THen I might use your roadmap to begin, but I really need to acquire skills toward the applications my employer desires. I might prefer to abandon the natural number game and focus on a functional programming approach, if I understand that better, or a system design approach, if that is more aligned with my skill set and previous experience.

Suppose I am an employer who wants to incorporate verification into my company (based on decision by management). I may need to spend some time understanding Lean well enough to vet applicants who will help with deployment of Lean in my organization. The roadmap might help with beginning implementations of toy examples or really really simple systems, but may not address my knowledge concerns at all. I might not find anything useful for a roadmap.

Suppose I practice mathematics and want to use tools to help further my research projects, but otherwise have little time or resources to do a deep dive into Lean. It may be to my advantage to skip the roadmap altogether and use agents or machines to do implementation for me: I would just need the minimal knowledge to spot check the results and ensure that results were not misforrmalized.

TL;DR it really helps to know what audience you intend to have for this document for it to be useful. Otherwise, do some market research (like your post can do) to find out what needs are not being fully addressed. You might draw some inspiration from the above scenarios.

Thanks for your thoughts. My objective is evangelistic, I guess. I am trying to market this to other people.

My target audience (@J. J. Issai (project started by GRP) ) would be junior software engineers with a high school mathematics education level and zero training in formal verification. I realize many people here came here of their own volition, seeking to learn.

Maybe this whole thread could have been reduced to a question like: "Why did you initially decide to pursue learning Lean and what kept you on the path? "

the lean language has a trackable timeline, with it being something that people have thought is unnecessary or difficult to adopt. Yet the community continues to grow at a rate that has been very surprising over the last little while. The thing I aim to combat is the genuinely curious individual who gets turned off by the idea, thinking the barriers to entry are too high for them to engage with.

The natural number game and other resources are great. I suppose I'm wondering if anyone here has found anything outside of the tools I have collected in this document to be useful or magnetizing.

I had one colleague who was trying the mathematics and Lean course and reported back that he couldn't make sense of how it applied and gave up on it For example.

Not saying it's a bad resource but just that there are many different perspectives and opinions on what is intriguing.

What has been intriguing to you and what do you think might be intriguing to others?

Complementary plug of The Mechanics of Proof if you didn’t know about it !

A more beginner friendly tome.

I agree “Mathematics in Lean” is more like “Lean for the working mathematician” , which entails in it a good amount of assumed mathematical maturity ( though at face value this isn’t obvious ).

@Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦

Thank you. This looks like a great resource. I don't think I've seen this one yet

Ty said:

A. Young said:

My target audience (J. J. Issai (project started by GRP) ) would be junior software engineers with a high school mathematics education level and zero training in formal verification. I realize many people here came here of their own volition, seeking to learn.

If that is your sole/primary audience, then you might focus on the algorithmic aspects of mathematics and logic. You might mention different types of verification (test, Hoare logic, loop invariants) and how they are treated, and then note that proofs of verification resemble proofs in mathematics, and that (certain kinds of) proofs of both can be embedded/expressed in a type system, with more flexibility if that type system allows for dependent types.

Then you have your AI generate working examples in Lean of very simple proof operations (e.g. for propositions A,B, and C, if you have a proof of ((A or B) implies C) and another proof of A, then you can make a proof of C), how inductive types enable proofs involving induction/recursion, and have the AI find/generate examples in Lean of common errors/misconceptions that occur. While there may be some underlying theory to be taught, many engineering- and science-minded folks like simple examples they can take in quickly and process. There are some tutorials in Lean like that, and I think the universe could do with a few more.

So building a friendly roadmap is one thing; having a friendly core of simple examples of good code and simple examples of bad code is even better.

@J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

Amazing, honestly. Thank you very much. This might be the most valuable feedback and insight I have received thus far.

Can you think of or perhaps offer any simple problems like you suggest?

I must admit I actually have tried this. I have some example problems that Ive been trialing with some friends/colleagues but haven't had much luck.

Curious what you might suggest. Maybe you/others here might have examples which appeal better than mine. hoare triples, test verification, and loop invariants is a good idea.

I went with a "puzzles" route and created a proof for a certain nuanced behavior in conways game of life.

I don't think its connecting well though. :sweat_smile:

One of my favorite examples demonstrates the "discontinuity" of formal language. (as far as I know, it is original with me.)

Write (and then prove) correctness of the following recurrence for Fibonacci numbers: f(n+1) = f(n) + f(n-1) . (Later you can discuss about whether using n+2,n+1,n or n,n-1,n-2 is better. ) Of course you need to build the for loop or recursive call around it, as well as declare f(2)=f(1)=1

Now contrast it with the following recurrence : f(n+1) = f(n + f(n-1)) . Discuss what goes wrong, and why, and how can such errors be detected, either automatically or by some other means. I think this is a core example of the need for validation.

You can comb the public parts of this Zulip for other small introductory examples.
